speechtext: Resuming debate with the hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in this debate at the third reading stage having participated in it at second reading.
I realize that there have been a few changes made to the proposed legislation as a result of the committee study. Essentially, we are still talking about the same fundamental issues that we were involved in then. That has really not changed.
I find it somewhat ironic, however, that something that has changed is the position of the Liberal party. That is not surprising since it was the original intention of the Liberal party to introduce this legislation under the Hon. Eugene Whelan about 10 years ago. At second reading we had the distinct impression that speakers for the Liberal party were in fact opposing this legislation for some very good reasons. Then, in committee, there seemed to be a softening of that position. Today, we have had speakers from the Liberal party speak on both sides of the issue.
Government Orders
Therefore it is somewhat confusing for the public and hon. members to determine what in fact the position of the Liberal party might be on some of these very fundamental questions.
I think it is impossible to separate the question of plant breeders' rights from the general trends which we see in agriculture, in rural Canada and in this government's approach to those issues.
Over the last number of years-certainly since the election of this government-we have seen a strong tilting away from involvement of the public sector in all aspects of the economy. Certainly, agriculture has not escaped that trend.
We saw it in large measure in large initiatives such as the free trade agreement, which represents a massive retreat on many fronts from public sector involvement. We also saw it in smaller instances, for example, the removal of oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. We saw a backing away from support for rural communities through the cuts of the government to the branch-line abandonment program. There are many other kinds of initiatives which this government has taken which really represent a fundamental shift away from public involvement in the economy.
In fact, that was a stated goal of this government when it was elected. In spite of its attempt to make it look like an incremental kind of movement it has been a steady movement, one which I think has started to present us with some trends that are clearly identifiable, trends which I think all Canadians can recognize.
I think part of those trends has been to make us more subject to pressure from international corporations, the whole multinational corporation structure that is more and more dominating the economy of the world. It is certainly dominating the agricultural economy.
Where have we seen that lead us in the province of Saskatchewan, my home province? We have seen an agriculture economy that has literally dived into the tank in the last number of years. We see farm foreclosures in record numbers. We see despair in the farm community, something that in my years of experience in the farm community I certainly have never seen before.

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
I had the opportunity to visit a farm community in southern Saskatchewan over the weekend. The people there were telling me that in the whole trading area for a town of about 500 people there were only three young families that have taken over farms in the last five or six years in that community. There is no way that three families on farms will be able to support a rural population in a community like that.
Right now we have seen a triple whammy, if you will, that has been directed at the farm community in Saskatchewan and, indeed, western Canada. We have seen the initial prices for grain come out at a drop of 12 per cent over what were already unacceptably low price. These are prices at which farmers can no longer afford to produce grain. These prices are no accident. They are part of the same trend that we see here in the plant breeders' rights legislation. They are part of the abandonment of the farm sector to control by corporations like Cargill and its equivalents around the world.
The second aspect of what has hit the farm community in the last very short period of time has been the rise in interest rates. In conjunction with that, the government has used its own lending agency, the Farm Credit Corporation, to inflict those same unacceptably high interest rates on farm families. It is ironical that an arm of the government that was originally intended, as I understand it, to provide long-term financial security to the farm sector by allowing farmers to borrow money at rates that could be sustained by farm operations should itself become a leader in increasing interest costs to farmers. This is making it more and more impossible for them to conceive of any future for themselves. It certainly discourages any young families from starting farming.
There is a story going around the farm community about a farm family being convicted of child abuse because it turned over the family farm to its children.
The third in this series of blows that has been inflicted on the farm community is the ping-pong game, the game of chicken that is being played between the federal government and provincial governments with respect to the payment which was promised to farmers to help them with their spring seeding. Clearly, we in the House have heard a whole series of announcements, a whole series of commitments and promises.
First, we were told by the Minister of Agriculture that there would be money in the hands of farmers before seeding time. As we got through January and February there was some backing away from that position. Then there was a definite promise that there would be a formal announcement of what kind of a program there would be, including who would get money and so on, before seeding time, certainly by the middle of April. Then we got into a very unseemly pushing match between the federal and the provincial governments. In spite of all those commitments we still do not have an announcement.
Piled on top of the high interest rates and the lower initial prices, we have federal and provincial governments still at odds over who shall pick up the cost of this program. This leaves farmers in the same vulnerable position vis-a-vis their financial situation as they were before. In fact, it might be even worse because with the passage of time decisions that need to be made are being increasingly delayed. The longer those decisions are delayed, of course, the harder it is to plan a farming operation for the future.
In this context I might add that the federal government says it cannot afford to compete with the treasuries of Europe and the United States. The provincial governments say they cannot afford to compete with the treasuries of Europe and the United States. Who is left competing with the treasuries of Europe and the United States? The farm families of Canada. Surely, their depleted bank accounts are the last place we can expect to find the financial muscle to compete with the treasuries of Europe and the United States.
Turning to the legislation before us, what is clearly at issue is that this particular legislation continues a trend that we have seen toward increasing control of the agriculture sector through the corporatization of the agriculture sector both now and into the future. There is a rapid increase in that kind of trend. I think we are on an exponential kind of curve where things that might now look fairly innocuous could very rapidly turn into much larger problems in the near future.
Some of the fundamental issues that remain at stake when we look at plant breeders' rights involve the concentration of corporate power and the relationship of that corporate power to the seed breeding and seed production industry.
May 3, 1990

We have heard about how seven out of ten of the major companies that are producing seed in the world are pharmaceutical and chemical companies. This is no accident. It is clear that these companies see a link between the chemical business and the seed production business. There is no reason for those links to develop without some expectation that they will be profitable to these companies.
We have seen a rapidly increasing concentration of power among those chemical and pharmaceutical companies. In the 1970s, there used to be 30 companies in the business of producing crop chemicals. We are now down to 12. The industry itself expects that by the turn of the century there will be only six of those kinds of companies left.
As the Minister of National Defence indicated, six or seven companies in a business does not represent a monopoly. Surely, that represents an oligopoly which amounts to much the same thing. It makes them vulnerable to the same kind of activities we see in the oil and gas business where there are regularly allegations of price fixing and so on.
Having only six or seven companies in a particular type of enterprise, especially when they are operating worldwide, leaves the whole business open to abuse, price-fixing and the development of trends which clearly will not benefit the thousands and thousands of small producers, especially the seed distribution companies that are relying on those companies for plant breeding.
Another issue is the access to seed varieties and the cost of seed to farmers. The hon. member pointed out that the pressure for this particular development has come from the large seed companies. Certainly, part of the agenda of those seed companies is to gain a larger share of control of the seed business. It is not hard to extrapolate that the day is rapidly coming when they will want to extend the need to pay royalties for the grain that farmers raise on their own farms which they hope to use for seed.
Those kinds of trends are already evident, for example, in Great Britain and other countries that have brought in this type of legislation. That would take away a very important source of seed for farmers across this country.
Government Orders
When it comes to cost, it erodes the contribution of the public at large to the costs of breeding and developing seeds in this country. The Minister of National Defence pointed out that as part of this legislation 60 per cent of the royalty payments will be returned to public plant breeding. However, it should be noted that that 60 per cent will no doubt replace money that is then cut in subsequent budgets from the general revenues of the government.
What will end up happening is that the rapidly diminishing number of farmers in this country will bear more and more of the cost of seed breeding and genetic development, while the public carries less of the burden. Surely, if we look at the income projections for farmers and farm families in this country, there is no good reason why those costs should be shifted so massively from the public sector to that very narrow base of financing which they provide. After all, the public at large benefits from the ongoing development of a healthy agricultural economy.
A second point that should be made with respect to plant breeding in this country is to remind the government of the old adage that if it ain't broke, why fix it?. We have had a very successful record of plant breeding. Plant breeding in Canada is held up world-wide as one of the most successful plant breeding systems in the world. The wheat and canola varieties that we have developed over the years have been world leaders in productivity and resistance to disease. It is clear that public plant breeding has more than demonstrated its worth. I found it interesting that the parliamentary secretary, who I believe is from Huron-Bruce, pointed out an example of successful plant breeding with regard to beans. That breeding was carried out under a public plant breeding program, which demonstrates again the relevance and the utility of a public plant breeding program in this country.
I think it is interesting to note as well that when major trials were undertaken in the state of North Dakota, whose growing, soil and economic conditions are very similar to the province of Saskatchewan, the publicly-bred varieties from Canada consistently out-performed those bred by private breeders from south of the border and from Europe. What we should be doing is giving a strong endorsement to that public plant breeding system,

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
rather than undermining it by introducing this legislation at this time.
The whole concern about where we are heading in the area of sustainable development is intensely relevant when it comes to this debate. We have seen the number of varieties of many types of crops around the world shrinking consistently. I refer to varieties that have been used on a large scale commercial basis. Corn and barley varieties are much smaller in number than they used to be.
It is quite clear that a healthy ecosystem requires many varieties of seeds to be used that are relevant to particular areas of the world and particular areas of the country. If we do not have that, we can become much more susceptible to different types of diseases and insect infestations and so on, which can wipe out large areas of our agriculture. This could have a large scale impact on major crops. The only way to avoid that is to ensure that there are large numbers of varieties that keep on being bred for particular conditions.
Placing more and more control in the hands of large multinational corporations which have only an interest in cutting down dramatically on the number of varieties is not good. The efficiencies of scale which make it possible for those companies to operate and which give them any kind of advantage at all requires that we limit the number of varieties that are available to as small a number as possible.
I would like to conclude by saying that I am concerned about the fundamental issues involved here. This legislation is another step on the road to corporate concentration in the whole agricultural field. The fundamental issues as I see them include the access and cost of seed to farmers, the impact on sustainable development and the undermining of the public sector involvement in the whole field of agriculture.
We in this party certainly believe that a modern, efficient farm sector based on the family farm model requires that we support public sector involvement, especially in an area as sensitive as the genetic strains that produce our seeds, which in turn produces our food-the life forms that we have in this country.
Therefore I urge the government to reconsider this legislation, even at this late stage. I urge Canadians to recognize the impact and to turn back the clock to a time when we were looking at agriculture as something that
required a significant commitment from the public sector. We must not abandon the family farm and the future of agriculture to the private sector and large multinational corporations.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? The hon. member for Mackenzie.

Madam Speaker, I note that the cost of enforcement of this particular piece of legislation has been raised once or twice today, rather obliquely. It occurs to me that perhaps the hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River might want to comment on the assertion from the government benches that this is a much more equitable way and that there was no other means of permitting the trade of plant varieties from one country to the other.
I point out to him something that I am sure he realizes. About two-thirds of the field crops which are sold in this country are sold as certified seed. Under our Seeds Act this requires that they be field inspected and subjected to an inspection at cleaning and bagging when they have a seal put on them. For most of the field crops that were grown in this country, there was really no big problem in getting contractual arrangements to test American or European-developed seeds. He has already pointed out that they do not do particularly well in western Canada, at least with his reference to the results in North Dakota.
Perhaps he could expand on his comments about the nature of international oligopolies where only a few very large firms control the trade from one country to another. They did not seem to think that this sort of contractual arrangement which, because of the power and requirement of the Seeds Act to have field and seed plant inspections, verifying how much seed of a variety was grown, made it vety easy for the original developer to collect its royalty. Why are we abandoning that perfectly workable system for international purposes to go beyond? Does he think that these companies have much more at stake than just making it easier to shift varieties from one country to the other?

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. He points out an element of this whole question of "If it ain't broke, why fix it?" The person here is only speculating, but I think that one of the reasons is that we are looking at trends here and so on.
May 3, 1990

The companies that are now pushing us down this road of plant breeders' rights and taking control of the seed industry also see some profitable aspects for themselves in controlling the inspection and contracting the inspection process. It makes it much easier for them to do some of this on an internal basis than it would otherwise be.
As we move farther down the road, the cost will increase rapidly for the kind of inspection and monitoring processes that we are going to have to put in place. As there becomes a larger and larger financial stake which these companies have in what particular seed is grown on what particular kind of farm, we will have to look at new compliance kinds of measures because the pressure will increase to implement measures that will ensure that every last dollar is wrung from the farmers when it comes to production of their crops and the provision of that seed.

Madam Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would care to comment on some testimony that was presented at committee stage from the Canadian Council for International Co-operation in a brief prepared on their behalf. They point out on page 2 of that brief dealing with plant patenting that in a few decades we have moved from intellectual property over plants to the patenting of micro-organisms and animals. Eluman cell lines and foetal tissue are not patentable in some countries. Recent European Economic Community and U.S. proposals either propose no upper limit to the patenting of life forms or draw the line only at the point of slavery. He spoke a little bit about trends. Some of those countries have moved very strongly in that direction.
I would close my comments by pointing out that in 1987 this particular group stated in its brief: "The U.S. and Japan proposed in 1987 that failure to provide patents be regarded as a non-tariff barrier to trade in the GATT round." This is the GATT round that we are currently in. "The U.S. went so far as to call upon countries to patent everything, including food, in their diplomatic note on this issue."
I wonder if he would care to comment on the assertions from other corners of this House that such things are simply guesses at the future when we have these
Government Orders
kinds of proposals before international bodies by countries at the international fora.

Madam Speaker, I would like to again thank the hon. member for his question.
As I said in the summation of my speech, what should concern us more than any other aspect of the legislation before us is the whole trend toward the patenting of life forms and the type of road that that takes us down. Surely there has to be some line drawn between where the community and public interests are clearly dominant, and not to be tampered with, and where activities that are carried on for private profit and private decision are made.
When we start extending those kinds of lines farther and farther in the patenting of different kinds of life forms, genes and so on, we are on a very slippery slope. The member is quite right to point out just how far on that slope we are has been clearly demonstrated at the GATT negotiations where the United States and Japan tried to lump in the patenting of life forms, food and so on with things like copyrights, television shows, intellectual property, the patenting of bicycles and automobile parts.
There is a line that needs to be drawn between life forms that we all depend on that are part of our ongoing existence and what is engaged in for private gain. The kinds of demands that have been made at the GATT negotiations are an indication of how far some countries have gone down this path. With the introduction of this legislation here and the closeness to which we are at passing it, we are just capitulating to a trend that we should be most actively resisting. The trend raises all kinds of moral and ethical questions besides the ones that we have raised in the context of agriculture and so on.

Mr. Speaker, it is appropriate today to speak of schizophrenia during National Mental Health Week. Schizophrenia strikes 1 per cent of the population and is a major illness in Canada. It takes up 6 per cent of hospital beds and costs over $3 billion annually in health care costs. Federal funds for research for this dreadful disease are less than $3 million annually-
Recent research in Canada has shown that schizophrenia is a biochemical brain disease in part caused by a genetic disorder. The quality of the research in Canada is outstanding, in spite of the low funding. Based on the progress that has been made in recent years, the chances of breakthrough are very good.
Because there is such a stigma attached to this illness, relatives and friends have provided support mostly in silence, hoping that a cure could be found. Now that this possibility appears achievable in our lifetime, this government should begin to make more of a commitment to research of this terrible disease.

Mr. Speaker, ten years ago, a group of students at the College Montmorency, which is in my riding, were made aware by their teacher, Serge Masse, of the widespread poverty in Haiti, aggravated by the aftermath of Hurricane Allen.
The students spontaneously took up an initial collection, followed by several more, which finally led to the students Haiti project. As part of this project, a group of students from the college went to Port-au-Prince, to work in two aid centres in 1982 and 1984-85, for periods of respectively three and four weeks.
In 1986, three students founded the organization Jeunes sans frontieres.
This year, thanks to substantial assistance from CIDA and the participants' own financial contribution, eight students will spend eight weeks in Burkina Faso, in Africa, to become familiar with social, cultural, political and economical realities in developing countries in the Third World.
Mr. Speaker, I say three cheers for the students at College Montmorency in Laval!

Mr. Speaker, largely because of this government's mean-spirited and persistent refusal to deal justly and fairly with a small Cree community in a remote settlement in northwestern Alberta, Canada now stands dishonoured before the world.
For more than 50 years the Lubicon Cree have been seeking a treaty settlement from the Canadian government sufficient simply to allow them, to the degree possible, to continue with their traditional way of life and, to the degree necessary, to build the required community infrastructure that may enable them to cope with technological culture we have thrust upon them.
For more than 50 years they have received nothing but delay, denial, deceit, and destruction.
Now the Human Rights Committee of the United Nations has determined the Canadian government's treatment of this small, embattled band to be unacceptable.
There is only one solution: the government must immediately resume negotiations with the Lubicon people, in good faith and without preconditions. Only the conclusion of a fair and just settlement will end this sordid chapter in our history and restore Canada's good name.

Mr. Speaker, the people of Duck Lake, Saskatchewan, have been keeping the history of the Northwest Rebellion alive for decades. In 1959, the Duck Lake Museum was founded to preserve the historical record of the events of 1885. It
May 3, 1990

is only the dedication and the commitment of the people of Duck Lake that has allowed this important heritage to be saved.
Now, with the help of the Western Diversification Fund, a new interpretive centre will be built. This will allow the people of Duck Lake to showcase an important part of Canadian history to many more people.
I think all Canadians owe the people of Duck Lake, Saskatchewan, a debt of gratitude for their efforts in protecting and giving new life to our Canadian past.

Mr. Speaker, Saturday, May 5, is a very difficult date for Soviet Jews in Leningrad. The ultra-nationalist group Pamyat is threatening a pogrom against the Jews of this city on Saturday.
As we know from the famous musical "Fiddler on the Roof" such threats have materialized in the past. This is a very frightening situation for the Jewish residents of Leningrad, as well as for their friends and relatives in Canada.
The Government of Canada has a moral responsibility to come to the aid of all Soviet Jews. We must use all diplomatic powers at our disposal to pressure President Gorbachev to control Pamyat and its anti-Semitic activities.
This government has a moral responsibility and indeed an administrative responsibility to process as quickly as possible all the immigration requests from the Soviet Union. I would ask this government not to wait to see what happens, but to do what it can while it can.

Mr. Speaker, unlike the Government of Canada, the Dutch government has tackled the environment head on. The Dutch environmental plan sets out targets and schedules, as well as the funds needed to achieve these goals.
The plan includes large reductions in pollution, be it sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides or carbon dioxide;
energy conservation; efficiency in residential heating and appliances; funds for energy efficiency and conservation; incentives for renewable energy generation; shifts to less polluting transportation modes; significant reductions in pesticides and fertilizers used in agriculture; and recycling of ozone-depleting gases.
In The Netherlands, there is political will to act. They did not stall, they did not shy away. They did not say, as Canada's energy minister did, that theirs is a small part of the global problem. The Dutch are giving leadership. When will the Government of Canada muster enough courage to at least emulate The Netherlands?

Nobody believes you!

Mr. Speaker, the evacuation of women, children and elderly from the Akwesasne reserve to Cornwall involved over 500 people. I wish to take this opportunity to thank Mayor Poirier and the various municipal officials and agencies in Cornwall, including the many local businesses and volunteers who came forward to assist those people who had to leave their homes as a result of the situation on the reserve.
As a resident of Cornwall, I saw first hand the amount of work and co-operation required. The project demanded considerable effort and resources. I was heartened by the willingness to help that was demonstrated by all parties. Grand Chief Mike Mitchell has already expressed his deep appreciation to the people of Cornwall.
I also wish to thank officials from Indian and Northern Affairs for their work and the management of the Transport Canada Training Institute in Cornwall for their part in the housing and feeding of the evacuees.
We all hope a permanent solution to the problem will be found soon and that this will enable the community of Akwesasne to live in peace.

GLOBAL ENVIRONMENT	*

Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon the Interparliamentary Conference on the Global Environment concluded four days of delibera-
May 3, 1990

tions. It was organized by members of the United States, including Senator Albert Gore.
There were interparliamentary delegations from 42 nations representing all continents and we adopted this marvellous report by consensus. It makes a number of important and internationally recognized recommendations.
On global climate change, there must be an immediate call to action for a 50 per cent reduction in greenhouse gases. We must reduce the deforestation of the planet, including all countries such as Canada, by 50 per cent. We must carry this message to our constituents and to our provinces. We must start replanting more than 30 million acres a year by the year 2000. There must be a total elimination of CFCs, methyl chloroform, carbon tetrachloride and halons. May 3, 1990
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the hon. member that we share his concern about high interest rates and their effects. We have to understand at the same time why these interest rates are there.
We are at the end of a long cycle of six years of growth. There are pressures in our economy which are very real and which are creating inflation. If we do not deal with that, interest rates will keep going higher all the time. We need to tackle inflation, and this is what the monetary policy is all about.

can underline the the fact that we are as concerned and as interested as the hon. member in seeing this cycle come to an end. We are doing what needs to be done to make sure that it comes to an end.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, that was certainly an eloquent representation that will not go unheeded.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-15, an act respecting plant breeders' rights, be read the third time and passed.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to participate in this third reading debate on Bill C-15 respecting plant breeders' rights.
I know that some members of the public are a bit puzzled by the name of this bill and some find it quite humorous. When you actually see the intent of this bill, Madam Speaker, you find that there is very little humour involved.
The reason I am so pleased to rise today is to once again express our unabated opposition to Bill C-15 and give a little history behind this. At the legislative committee stage, my colleague from Mackenzie tried to amend the legislation to be certain that there would be a check to ensure that all stakeholders in the plant breeders industry be consulted by the minister. We wanted reports each year so that the plant breeding community in

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
Canada, which is a large industry, would have some sort of government monitoring.
Curiously, the Liberals would not support our amendment so we in the New Democratic Party are alone in this. The Liberals have consented to go along with the government in support of Bill C-15 and we in the New Democratic Party are alone in our opposition. Our reasons for doing so are numerous.
Several developments have occurred in the plant breeders' rights area. A research study by North Dakota State University found that Canadian commercial varieties of grain tended to out-perform most American varieties across the state. My colleague from Mackenzie spoke about this in February in a statement in the House. According to the study, Canadian commercial varieties of wheat, oats, durum, rye, barley and flax tended to out-perform most American varieties across that state.
My colleague's analysis is that Bill C-15, introduced by this government and now supported by the Liberals, will mean that Canadian farmers who farm under unique soil conditions in the north will lose the advantage they now enjoy with public plant breeding. They will now be forced to depend on the same so-called world scale profit-oriented research that was proven so inadequate in the Dakotas. Our hesitation about supporting this bill has already been proven to have great credibility. That is on the domestic market.
We also have reasons on the international scene to oppose this bill. I would like to focus on those. I would like to outline the four principal reasons why we are opposing this bill. They are: one, the intellectual property rights question; two, the concern for the community of intellectual property rights, otherwise known as the informal innovation system, a north-south question; three, the whole trade question; and four, the concept of genetic erosion. In the time that is left to me I would like to expand on those four categories that outline our concern.
On the intellectual property rights, that is a very insidious element to this bill and although plant breeders' rights sounds like a science fiction creation, perhaps an "R" rated one, we see that it is in that whole domain. While it may still seem like science fiction, we are moving rapidly into a world where transgenetic species are becoming common. That is that you cannot distinguish between what is a plant and what is an animal. The technical or scientific distinctions between plants and animals have always been blurry. UPOV, the Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants, has conceded this point. There is no clear, well-defined borderline between plants and animals so there is an economic hesitation about getting involved with patenting life forms. There is also a moral consideration, and it is this moral consideration that leads the number of church organizations to withhold their approval of such initiatives.
The second of my principal reasons for opposing this bill is the concern for the community, the concern for the Third World farmer. This is the north-south argument against Bill C-15. The intellectual property rights which we see intrinsic in this bill are of the philosophical framework of the north. This bill does not recognize that southern farmers-those plant geneticists I met with when I went to Africa and Eritrea in northern Ethiopia, the bread basket of the world, where a number of life forms which we have benefited from in the developing world, but they were developed there-those farmers should be paid in some way for their resources, their centuries of developing the plant species. We just come in, pillage what they have, bring it back and make a profit from it. It does not hold true, if we are going to use our philosophical framework, that it should be a market organization that should be determining that we have a responsibility to reimburse those farmers for all those centuries of labour and skill in developing those plant species. In effect, what we should be doing is demanding that the north recognize farmers' rights through a tax-based payment to the FAO international fund for plant genetic resources.
Bill C-15 does nothing to do that. My colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie, tried very hard to bring about an amendment at the committee stage on this very issue. Our concern is about the plundering of Third World germ plasm and the possibility, as was raised by Patrick Mooney, one of the world-recognized experts in this field, that the union for the protection of new varieties convention should render germ plasm subject to biotechnology patents in the north. That is the second major area of our concern.
The third area of concern is under a heading that is very familiar to this House as it is very much within our own philosophical framework and will be recurring over
May 3, 1990

and over again in the days to come and that is international trade.
We have many reservations about becoming involved in this global economy because we feel it is not to our advantage. Nowhere is that more evident than in this bill. We are not the big players. We are the ones that are being made the Third World.
Bill C-15 is the first step toward full compliance with the proposed system of international trade under the GATT. What Canada decides to do with this bill will influence how developing countries judge their legal options. So, as the critic for international development, I can see that Canada is capitulating to the dominant economic forces.
We have given away our moral leadership in defending the developing countries and we are going along with those countries that really believe that the more money you have, the more power you have, the better you are. I had hoped that Canada would resist that dynamic.
The final area of opposition is one that I hold very close to me and that is the whole area of genetic erosion. As a member of this Parliament's Environment Committee we are constantly being given evidence of the kind of global environmental crisis which we face. Bill C-15 is only just going along with that trend and not addressing it in any way that helps us toward a solution.
Our farmers are being pushed very, very hard by economic circumstance to make choices they would otherwise not like to make. Those problems are all the more dramatic in the developing world. We are being pushed, both here and internationally, to erode our environmental capital.
We are being pushed by the dynamics that I cited in previous portions of this address to do mono-cropping, to do cash cropping, to get involved in the global economy, and we are using up our environmental capital.
The genetic erosion that is of concern to me is no more evident than in Africa. The people who I saw in northern Africa managed quite well over the centuries until we got our sticky fingers in there and decided that they should grow cash crops. We now see the kind of social erosion which results in war, which causes more social erosion, which runs into "Well, you have to get into the
Government Orders
global economy; you are going to have to put in structural adjustment; we are going to help you poor folks but you are going to be playing by our rules". The result is mono-cropping and the deterioration of the genetic resource.
One of the most passionate opponents to plant breeders' rights legislation has been Sir Otto Frankel of Australia, a scientist long involved in genetic conservation. He has decried the genetic provisions in this bill. Just as I have said, it is the commercial, hence the biological monopolies, which stifle genetic diversity. By encouraging the developing world to buy into the market system, we are encouraging them to use their environmental capital.
We have done it to our own native peoples here in Canada. We have somehow come with a great deal of ego, thinking that we know best how the native people of our land should be running their economies. Only now are we adopted some humility, to admit we have really messed up. I think that same degree of humility should be adopted with regard to the Third World because we are messing up there too with mono-cropping and the elimination of biological diversity.
We believe that the passage of plant breeders' rights legislation contributes directly to genetic erosion.
Of course, I care what is happening on the the farms of Canada. 1 am concerned about the farmers who feel that their options are limited by the economic circumstance in which they find themselves and by the trade policies which this government has imposed on them by adoption of the free trade deal.
I am also concerned about our world. It is not just Canada that we should be worried about. I have said repeatedly that we are seeing the very beginnings of a global consciousness environmentally, but we have not quite reached that consciousness politically and socially.
If this government adopts this Bill C-15 then I think it will only make the lives of Third World farmers more miserable. It will only increase the devastation to the environment of the developing countries. How can we expect the Third World to participate as equal partners in the crisis that is facing us if we do not give them the assistance to become that full partner. The adoption of this bill would be a repudiation of the Third World. It would mean that we are willing to go along with the

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
process and many other such initiatives of this government.
Our opposition is firm. It is with extreme disappointment that I see that the Liberal party has capitulated to the market philosophy that this bill is necessary. Even if Third World countries do not have plant breeders' rights legislation, they are not immune from the pressures our Canadian farmers have felt. Dr. James Thomas, formerly with Agriculture Canada and now with a consortium for international development notes that Bolivia is already feeling the effects of reduced source of seed competition because the multinationals have already purchased a number of smaller suppliers and then only provide one most profitable line from among those purchased.
This bill is just a blank cheque to the multinationals to come in and take the resources and make lots of money without giving any to the people who developed those resources originally. It is very much, as my colleague, the member for Mackenzie has pointed out, the plundering of Third World resources.
In conclusion I would like to reiterate that we in the New Democratic Party are strongly opposed to this bill for economic reasons, moral reasons and international development reasons.
The four points I have made throughout this address were: first, intellectual property; second, the farmer's rights in the developing world to have recompense for their development of seed varieties that we have used to our profit; third, the whole trade dynamic and the globalization of trade; and fourth, the genetic erosion.
Madam Speaker, this will be a sad day if Bill C-15 is passed. I know that the amount of mail that I have received on this issue has been disproportionate to the amount of knowledge that exists out there in the community. The people who know about this know the consequences of this legislation, and the are very active in their communities. They will continue to make the Liberal party very uncomfprtable in supporting this legislation. Our position in our party is clear. We think this is a bad bill. It is a bad bill for Canada and it is a bad bill for the world.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for an excellent speech on a subject that is not only of grave importance to this country, but to the world as well, as she so ably pointed out.
I was wondering if the hon. member could pursue how deeply we are indebted to the agriculturalists of the Third World for having protected over the centuries, quite literally, the gene pool?

Madam Speaker, I am only too pleased to speak from personal experience on that question.
When I was in Africa in 1986 working for OXFAM Canada, I went to northern Ethiopia, to what Ethiopians call the country of Eritrea. It was a country at war, a country devastated by famine. What I saw there in a number of places were agricultural experimental farms doing miraculous things under very, very hard circumstances.
Madam Speaker, you have seen the television images of that country that has been devastated by famine. I am sure that your imagination can go on from there.
Those agricultural experimental farms were the product of centuries of knowledge. The people of Eritrea in northern Ethiopia have, through their skill and through their knowledge, developed seed varieties that are particularly successful in that area. It was like a garden of Eden in northern Ethiopia. Those people are the ones to whom we should be very grateful.
Ethiopia was the breadbasket of the world, as I said in my address. Now that we are encouraging the developing world to become part of the global economy, we are forcing that knowledge away from them. We are taking it. We are stealing it. We are using it and not paying for it.
As I said, this plant breeders' rights legislation forces the Third World into a weakened position. Hundreds and thousands of people were dependent upon the seed varieties that were used at the little experimental farm I saw in northern Ethiopia.
This is where the morality of this bill comes in. If we are willing not to pay them for their resources, then we have a responsibility to assist them with food aid, with increased development assistance and other options. We
May 3, 1990

are doing none of that, because we do not want to get involved with the political complications of that country.
When we try to get the interlink going, as I have done in both the external affairs committee and the environment committee, it is met with a great deal of frustration.
I thank the member for his question. It is a very good one. We always feel very good about the kind of assistance we give overseas, but we have to look at the big picture. We have done very well from their resources. We have profited from them, and we are not paying for them.

Madam Speaker, I would like to pursue this matter further with the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands. She made it very clear where the varieties of wheat, in particular, originated, as well as some of the other cereals. Northern Ethiopia and the general area of northeast Africa is the centre for much of the genetic diversity in those cereals, particularly wheat.
Just as an aside, the opening of western Canada was made possible by the introduction of a variety from northern Kenya, not too far from that area. It has been fairly successfully economically in turning that area into a breadbasket as well.
She made it quite clear how the farmers through selective breeding have continued to keep a wide diversity of varieties and a big genetic pool of material available for everyone on the globe to use.
I did not finish hearing the story about how the northern countries are now changing the law so that they can patent the plants that they develop from these varieties and then force the Ethiopians and Eritreans to pay a royalty if they decide to use the results from those plants for their commercial farms. The same thing is happening in Peru and Bolivia, which is also a centre for diversity for other types of plants.
This is the point that we have been trying to make, and the hon. member has made it veiy well. Would she tell us what she thinks of making the north-south split even stronger by changing the rules for the northern countries, giving them a very big advantage economically over those countries that have been so forthcoming and giving of their thousands of years of looking after those plants and that genetic material?

Madam Speaker, I thank the member for Mackenzie for that question. He was veiy forceful in the legislative committee to try to get accepted an amendment that would have prevented this from happening, an amendment that would have recognized the very large gift that we have received, or that there is a reciprocal arrangement. It is a gift, if we pay for it. It is theft if we do not. That is exactly what is happening.
Dr. Otto Frankel, the Australian geneticist, has been, as I said in my address, very passionate in his opposition to this legislation for that very reason.
Environment Canada says a lot of nice words about genetic diversity. Why can Agriculture Canada not see the same thing? There is a sort of contradiction here. One wonders whether the left hand knows what the right hand is doing.
If we are going to be environmentally sensitive we have to understand that that must extend beyond our borders, and that the kind of economic advantage that we have in Canada carries with it a large degree of responsibility. The adoption of this bill is the abrogation of that responsibility.

Madam Speaker, it seems to make very little difference what government bill we rise to speak on in this House. The reasons given by the government for having to bring them in essentially boil down to a matter of economics. In many instances that is one of the major rationales that the government has mentioned for bringing forward legislation.
The plant breeders' rights bill is no different. I would suggest that in addition to the pleas for fiscal responsibility that it is also merely a way of furthering the Conservative agenda which is a matter of privatization. Bill C-15, if nothing else, is precisely that. It is the privatization of the genetic furtherance of plants in this country. Of course the government is so fond of saying that it goes beyond that, as it does with the GST. It says: "There are 40 countries that have brought in a GST so we have to do it".
It is not able to say that there are that many countries around the world which have brought in plant breeders' rights legislation. There are 18. Even so, the small number of 18 is a sufficient number for the government to use as the reason for bringing in plant breeders' rights. I would say that the me, too, issue is just another part of the smoke and mirrors which is an excuse for the government to do what it wants to do, which is to

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
privatize and deregulate. Certainly, deregulation is part of it as well.
If this government thinks that it is going to be able to have as much control over the breeding, proliferation and even the transportation of plants, cereal grains and so on across the border as it has now, then it is certainly very much mistaken.
As has already been mentioned by other hon. members, it was shown by the United States agricultural people that plants and cereal grains developed in the United States under this privatized system of raising plants in trying to help cereal grain growers come to grips with problems, whether environmental or bacterial, is not as efficient. The United States agriculturalists found that Canadian-bred cereals were superior to those which were developed in the United States. My party and I have maintained, and a good many other organizations which I shall mention subsequently have verified, that cereal grains developed in Canada are superior.
During the course of some of the speeches by government members at a previous debate in the Elouse, I was not surprised that the idea of the budget was mentioned. As I said, there does not seem to be any area where they do not seem to be able to work in the need to cut costs. I would suggest that this is one more case where it can be demonstrably shown that this government is penny wise and pound foolish, as the saying goes, and I will get to that a little bit later.
There is ample evidence to show that the way plants have been developed is cost-effective for Canada, as well as for other people around the world, whether it is matter of being able to grow the crops, or because Canada is a rather large supplier of cereals to the world.
I suggest that there are other instances where the government has demonstrated that it is penny wise and pound foolish. One such instance relates primarily to the concept of research. In spite of all the fine-sounding rhetoric that we have heard from the government in relation to scientific development, and in particular, references to its Centres of Excellence, it really does not have much of an idea what really constitutes research. It certainly does not recognize it when it occurs.
I would like to refer quickly to something all together out of the field of agriculture, for a moment. In retrospect, I do not see how Canadians can help but realize- although this government does not-that what really occurred with the aircraft companies Canadair and de Havilland was really investment in research by the people of Canada. For the government to have sold off and privatized the production of aircraft in Canada was nothing more than the giving away of a tremendous amount of research done and paid for by Canadians. It was done with the marvellous expertise that we have developed. I cite those as examples to show that this government really does not know what on earth research is.
However, there is an even better example of this, which illustrates that the whole concept is endemic within the Conservative party and that it goes back a long way. That is precisely what happened to the Arrow aircraft. A previous Conservative government did pretty much the same thing with it as it did with Canadair and de Havilland. It gave away Canadian expertise. Actually, in that case it did not give it away, it burned it and cut it up with a cutting torch. Those very expert Canadians who had developed that magnificent flying machine then went to the United States and, in good measure, assisted in putting the Americans on the moon.
I will get into some of the specifics of what I see has happened with respect to research in agriculture in Canada in a moment in a context similar to the one I just referred to involving the aircraft industry.
We have predictions that this measure is going to be a panacea for Canadian agriculture. It is going to make Canadian agriculture more efficient and more productive. We have heard these kind of predictions before. We have heard these kind of predictions in relation to our forestry, and look what is happening there. Our forests are being depleted at a rate from which it will be impossible to recover.
Even more obviously-and in relation to incidents which happened in the maritimes as recently as yesterday-we are hearing the same kinds of glowing predictions in relation to the fishery. These are predictions which we have received from this government in previous years-certainly ever since it came to power in 1984 and while the Conservatives sat in opposition. We
May 3, 1990

heard all the things that they would be doing if they were in government.
We have seen as a result of government actions that it has devastated the forestries and the fisheries. I would suggest that there is no reason in the world why we should in any way assume that its predictions in so far as what will happen if plant breeders' rights are instituted in this country that the results will be any different.
The assurances that we are going to become productive and efficient are just not anything that we can take any stock in at all, as was the case with other programs which the government brought in since the last election. I have a particular specific interest in unemployment insurance. We have seen, again, that the government claims in the most glowing of terms that Canadian workers are going to benefit enormously because of the changes to the unemployment insurance program. The results are precisely the opposite. Hundreds of thousands of Canadians are not going to be eligible to receive unemployment insurance at all. Thousands and thousands more than that are going to find that their benefits will be reduced as a result of this government's changes.
This brings me back again to the idea of cuts, cuts, cuts. Considering all the references to the budgetary problems of the government in relation to this particular debate which have been made, one of the main reasons that it is bringing in plant breeders' rights legislation at this time is that it does not like to see public money going into a marvellous Canadian government department, that of Agriculture Canada.
Something that we western Canadians appreciate is that 88 per cent of the grain and oilseed stocks in western Canada are a result of the development of those stocks within Agriculture Canada. I come from Saskatoon. I know very well that the past history of the development of these varieties and the diversification of varieties in Canada is in no small measure a direct result of the research which has gone on at the University of Saskatchewan which is in the city, part of which I represent.
I would like to point out in another context how enormously beneficial for all of Canada is public participation in the furtherance of scientific development in our community. We are all very well aware-and sometimes we have slightly differing views-of the oil sands projects in Alberta. Should we develop megaprojects or should we not? Most Canadians are probably not aware that the technology for the extraction of oil from the tar sands was not developed by Shell Oil, or Imperial Oil, and certainly not by Petro-Canada, which was not in existence at the time, or by Sun Oil, which is one of the
Government Orders
major operators in northern Alberta around the city of McMurray, but by the Northern Alberta Institute of Technology. Public money is what developed the ability of the Canadian oil industry to be doing what it is in the tar sands of northern Alberta.
We have a similar example in the Department of Agriculture. It was the Canadian public agricultural research institutions in Canada which led to the worldwide use of canola as feed and as an oil product. The crop now known as canola, and formerly called rape, was used for its oil. That oil was poisonous and was used as an industrial lubricant particularly during the war when there were problems with the availability of petrochemical substances usually used for lubrication.
It was technology from these public research institutions that led to the modification of that crop from the point where it was poisonous as an oil to people and livestock, as was the meal, to the point where it is now sought as both a meal and as a consumable oil for livestock and people on a world-wide basis.
What the government is proposing through this legislation is a move away from that concept. I would not say that it is a uniquely Canadian concept. I would say that it is a concept within our country solely consistent with our nature as Canadians to develop these kinds of things not only for our own benefit-and certainly not with the prime requisite that it be profitable-but for the benefit of the community in which the research is done, and that it serve the world-wide community. That has been demonstrably the case whether we are talking about the development of insulin or about the modification of rape into canola, from a poisonous substance into an entirely edible substance by animals and humans in the form of oil or meal.
As well the evidence is that multinational corporations are not something with which we as Canadians have had a tremendous amount of positive experience. The fact of the matter is that when this bill goes through, what we are going to be looking at is a concentration in the hands of multinational corporations whose primary interest is the development of seeds and crops, along with the development of fertilizers and pesticides to go along with them. It comes down to a question of why would we turn our source of food supply over to some organizations over whom we have so little control?

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
There is no evidence that the multinational corporations which are so involved in the grain industry and in the chemical and pesticide industry have the interests of the Canadian public as their primary interest. In fact, there is evidence which will indicate-and we will get closer and closer to the threshold-that even human genes are being introduced into some plant and animal varieties.
This morning I heard some questioning from the government side with respect to the veracity of this type of scenario. If there is anyone on either side of the House who thinks that the introduction of cereal grains, oilseeds and other plants as well into our agricultural industry, whereby the companies will not be able to breed them in such way that they are specifically resistant to only their chemicals-whether they be fertilizers, pesticides, or herbicides-then I suggest that such a person certainly does not have a very good grasp of the kinds of mentality, the kinds of thinking, the kinds of imagination, if you will, within the laboratories of the companies involved in pesticides, plant breeding and fertilizing within this nation.
I would like to refer to some of the organizations. This morning one of the members opposite disparaged the remarks of a Mr. Mooney. Mr. Mooney was speaking on behalf of several organizations. I would just like to read off a few of them, if I may. The inference was that he was only one person speaking for one person. This is who Mr. Mooney was speaking for.
He was speaking for the National Farmers' Union, the Canadian Catholic Organization for Development and Peace, the Canadian Environmental Law Association, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Council of Canadians, Ecology Action Centre, Friends of the Earth, Friends of the Rainforest, GATT-Fly, Inter Pares, the Manitoba Council for International Co-operation, the Marquis Project, Mouvement Agriculture Biologique au Quebec, Ecological Agriculture Projects of MacDonald College, McGill University, One Sky, Oxfam-Canada, Saskatchewan Council for International Co-operation, Ten Days for World Development, the United Church of Canada, Wild West Organic Harvest Co-op and World Inter-Action.
My concern is the same as the concern of those people. I thank you very much for your attention, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I know very little about plant breeders' rights, just as my hon. colleague knows nothing about lamprey eels. So we are on a similar plane.
I am certainly glad that I spent the 20 minutes here to listen to his speech, because I have learned a great deal. I think that the members across the way have also learned a great deal. My hon. colleague is very convincing and persuasive. I am just wondering why we are alone in opposing this particular bill and why the Liberals are not with us. It is very mindful of the GST.
What is the rationale for the government putting forward this bill? Why are they for it? In just a few words, tell us why it is for this bill?

Madam Speaker, the answer is rather obvious. We come back to the same motivation which fuels the engine of the government opposite, privatize. A good portion of development has been exemplary worldwide by Canadians in many different fields.
The reason I went far afield from agriculture was to emphasize the contribution that Canadians have made, sometimes a little more specifically to our own society, in relation to some of the smaller aircraft companies which I did not mention. We did just toss them away for a pittance, after having spent enormous sums of money on them. It is a matter of privatization. This government cannot stand the public sector being so obviously successful as it has been in the development of agricultural crops and so on within this country.
I really have no explanation why the government cannot stand this, except that I suppose it sees a potential for profit because it is obvious that once this bill passes, the profit motive will become the engine which fuels the development of agricultural crops within this country. The fact that Agriculture Canada will receive 60 per cent royalty on crops which it develops does not come anywhere near to ameliorating the devastation that is going to occur as a result of this
May 3, 1990

deregulation. This is another reason for the government doing this. It is not only privatization, it is deregulation.
Then you get companies such as Cargill. It is unbelievable the amount of money the government of Saskatchewan is guaranteeing to this company, a company which last year made a $35 billion profit. I would suggest, Madam Speaker, that this is about seven times larger than the provincial debt and is sufficient to be able to buy out the province of Saskatchewan along with its debt.
Not coincidentally, the money going to the Cargill corporation is for the development of a fertilizer plant. Although if you were to simply look at the commodity markets around the world, you would think it was a mere trader in grain. Of course, it goes far beyond that. It is a matter of privatization and deregulation and getting the government out of involvement in this. Profit for the private sector, that is what it is all about.

Madam Speaker, when the history of this Parliament is written, I would not be surprised if this bill that the House is poised to adopt today will prove to be one of the most important pieces of legislation and one which stands to its great discredit.
The fact is it is going to be adopted because both the Conservative government and the Liberals are determined that it should go through. It is only the New Democratic Party that is standing in this House to oppose this Draconian piece of legislation. It is very interesting to me that, perhaps because of all the furore over issues like the GST, free trade, UI, and Meech Lake which have dominated the news, it is a bill like this which may, in the end, have the most profound effect on the lives of future generations of Canadians and of millions of people around the world.
Bill C-15 has the effect of causing Canada to join with other predominantly western countries to privatize a very key area of life on the planet, the development and control of seed and plant genes. If this bill passes it will set conditions on the sale of what is bred and of what is discovered. It will provide an effective subsidy to trans-
Government Orders
national corporations and it will apply effectively an industrial patent system to living things.
It has been interesting to me that the bill, notwithstanding the lack of general attention given, has nonetheless generated very considerable concern across the country. From my own constituency of Victoria, I have received many, many letters from people expressing their grave concern about this bill and I would like to put some of them on the record. I hope I am not embarrassing anyone by including them in the record of Hansard. I have a letter from Mary Lanceley who writes:
I understand that Bill C-15, which relates to the patenting of seeds is about to be pushed through the Commons while nobody is looking. It will put the control of the sale and the development of seeds into the hands of a few large companies. Most of these companies also are related to petrochemical and pharmaceutical branches. It stands to reason that the seeds developed and sold by these companies will be those which require increased use of fertilizers and pesticides. Old reliable seeds will no longer be available. This poses an increased threat of chemical pollution in our environment and further toxicity of the food we eat.
The letter concludes:
Many people are alarmed, and rightly so, at the threat of extinction of various kinds of animals; we should be equally concerned about seeds. We will lose some irreplaceable plant stock if this horrendously wrong bill is allowed to pass.
I have a letter from Richard Johnston and Esther Muirhead from Victoria which reads:
I strongly oppose Bill C-15 and I want you to stop its passage.
The Plant Breeders' Rights Bill will allow a few international corporations involved in plant breeding to control privately, research and decision-making regarding the genetic material upon which we all rely. These corporations are closely linked to the petrochemical fertilizer industry.
The Third World is at risk of losing ancient seed strains in the push toward cash production of food crops for urban populations. Locally rich and diverse and often undocumented varieties of seeds that resist certain local pests and diseases will be threatened by the freedom of corporations to patent new seed varieties they develop or discover.
And, in effect, I may add, to control the release of those varieties. The writers go on:
The extinction of genetic material on this planet is increasing daily; control of the preservation of genetic diversity needs to remain in the hands of public institutions.

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
One more letter from M. Johnson who writes:
I have just heard about a disturbing bill and am told it is rapidly approaching its third and final reading while most Canadians remain ignorant of it. I wish to direct your attention to Bill C-15 and express concern about the failure to inform Canadians about this bill. It has enormous ramifications for us all in terms of health and environmental concerns both locally and globally. As such it deserves a fair and public hearing across Canada. This bill, although it seems non-threatening on the surface is a very dangerous one in reality. As it will only be a benefit financially to a small number of chemically based multinational corporations it clearly is not in the best interests of the Canadian public. I do not understand how a government that openly declares a genuine concern for the fate of our environment can then offer this invitation to chemically based corporations to further monopoly of our food supply.
I want to deal with a number of specific concerns about the plant breeders' rights bill. The first is the effect of the patent on life forms. I simply cannot believe that the government and the Liberals understand the precedent that this bill creates. We are told there is no scientifically detectable difference between the genetic material of plants and those of animals. Transgenetic technologies are already in place and already being used. The legal definition of plants will begin to blur into the legal definition of life forms. The precedent which this bill creates imposes a challenge and a threat in the long run to the very existence of life itself because it offers the first legal step toward the ownership of a key form of life, a form of life which is not distinguishable from that of animals.
I put the question to the Elouse: the world's plant resources are a common heritage; should one segment of our society have private control over this precious and vital resource through the use of patents? That is the issue in this bill and that is why we are opposing it with all the force that we can muster in this House.
A second concern is that of corporate concentration which this bill encourages and on which Canada has now folded in front of a multinational corporate drive to control plants and seeds on the planet. Of 10 major international seed companies, eight are incorporated with transnational petrochemical and pharmaceutical companies. They are the Royal Dutch Shell, Union Carbide, Monsanto, Ciba-Geigy, Upjohn and other big business conglomerates which have been acquiring hundreds of seed companies over the past 20 years. When they get the power in Canada that this bill gives them, they will join that with the power they have
acquired in other countries to completely control the development of seed life in the planet.
Conglomerate food processing corporations are already dabbling in the seed business indicating the push toward corporate control from seed to table. In 1970 in Britain when they adopted the equivalent of this legislation, within a week 84 small seed companies were bought out by one multinational giant.
The European Economic Community, which has similar legislation, recently issued a catalogue of what was permitted in terms of seeds. The effect of that catalogue was to make illegal over 2,000 vegetable varieties in England and Europe. To sell them would be violating a patent owned by one of the corporate seed merchants.
The Liberals and Conservatives who are supporting this bill simply cannot understand the impact it will have on the environment and the effect on the extinction of genetic material. Already the diversity of crops on this planet is threatened in the same way that other industrial developments are threatening animal and bird life on the planet.
This bill is a companion to the impact of the industrial revolution on the global planet. If we step back from the monster that science has created and ask what we are doing to control those developments, we find that with this bill we are not only accelerating the development of the control and reduction of seed and plant variety, we are turning it over to private multinational conglomerates. We are taking out of democratic public control the need to ensure a diversity of genetic pool on the planet.
In 1978 Great Britain lost 700 non-traditional synonyms, which are varieties very much alike. Since then Britain has lost 874 varieties which prior to the adoption of their legislation were distinct, stable and uniform and had a quality of value to gardeners in Britain. Erna Bennett, a former staff member of the Food and Agricultural Organization in the United States, estimates that 75 per cent of vegetable varieties currently planted in Europe will be extinct by 1991 if current policy is continued.
By the year 2000, which is only a decade away, the FAO estimates that two-thirds of all plant seeds planted in the Third World will be of uniform strains. We are losing our genetic reservoirs which are our built-in production against changes in climate or the ecology of the world's food-growing lands. We have already heard in this debate the connection that this bill sets up with the
May 3, 1990

chemical industry and the direction that this goes. Presently there are 4,000 registered pesticides in Canada. With this bill we will add to the danger that by some chemical fluke we will suddenly wipe out a whole food strain or a whole plant strain. The sale of chemicals to control pests and disease has increased 32-fold in 35 years and is now a major threat to the plant life in North America.
My colleague from Saanich-Gulf Islands added yet another point which was critical to the consideration in this debate, and that is the effect on people in the Third World. We are really joining a consortium of already rich countries to further choke off the potential for self-sustainable agricultural development in the Third World and to further build a monopoly that will cause increased poverty and economic degradation in the Third World. Ninety-five percent of all global human nutrition is derived from only 30 plants, all of which originate in the Third World.
Over the century, the knowledge and skill needed to carefully select individual seeds for the next planting have been the specialized domain of subsistence farmers-mostly women, I may say. This heritage is simply not recognized by this bill and its companion pieces in other countries. It is the heritage that has given the world its basic genetic material for most of the food which is grown around the world today.
Bill C-15 would give the right to private companies to patent, not only seeds which they develop, but the seeds which they discover. If this bill is allowed, the valuable natural resources located in the world's poorer nations will become wide open for exploitation by these private multinational corporations, based primarily in the rich north. Most of the fruits, vegetables, crop plants grown in the world have come to us from hundreds of generations of careful selection and cultivation which has been carried on by agriculturalists all around the world. This bill seeks to use the sovereign power of this legislature to turn over into private hands the control of that development in the generations ahead.
There is little wonder that this bill has generated opposition, not only in Canada, but from around the world. Organizations within the UN system, the UNEP, FEW, UNESCO, UNCTAD, WHO, the World Food
Government Orders
Council and the Brundtland Commission, all of these international organizations oppose this development. This House should listen to the agricultural organizations throughout Canada and around the world.
My friend from Saskatoon-Dundurn outlined the number of international development organizations in Canada, including OXFAM Canada, that have opposed this bill. It is opposed by universities, and by individuals who have been reading the provisions of this bill, listening to the discussion, and understanding that this bill must not pass this Parliament. It has not received the attention it deserves across this country.
In conclusion, I say that when the history of this Parliament is written, it will be the vote of those members who support this bill who will be remembered by future generations as one of the great mistakes they have made in this Parliament.
Hear, hear!
It is a bad bill. It ought not to be passed. [Translation]
