It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The hon. member for New Westminster- Burnaby (Ms. Black)-REAL Women; the hon. member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons)-Air Canada; the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur (Mr. Arse-neault)-Forestry development.

Madam Speaker, I was amazed at some of the information that the hon. member from Victoria included in his remarks.
The information regarding the number of varieties that have literally been declared illegal in countries where similar legislation was introduced previously is very useful. Many varieties of vegetables and so on were simply no longer available to people because, presumably, the companies that held the patents for these seeds decided that they would no longer be on the market.

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
I am wondering if the member could expand on the process that is in place in those countries that would literally take existing plant varieties off the market. Would he remind the House of the dangers of that kind of activity happening here?

Madam Speaker, I am pleased that the member asked me the question, but I have to confess a certain nervousness as he begins to plumb the depths of my knowledge of some of the details of this bill.
I will take a shot at it. I am learning that in this place-particularly associated, as I am, with members from Saskatchewan-that it is possible to talk for at least 20 minutes on a subject that one does not know as much about as one might like. I am fully persuaded of the importance of this bill, and that represents my independent judgment. I certainly do not back off any of the remarks that I made in my speech.
As well, the process that has been operating here and that gives effect to the development to which my hon. friend refers is very clear. Quite simply, when a bill like this passes, the large multinational corporations that are already in the field, particularly the seed companies, get the advantage of this, acquire a patent and ownership of the particular seed and its relatives, and then control the market. These are primarily seed companies but also other companies that are getting into the business and that are part of the consumer food chain, or in the business of selling fertilizers and related products. These corporations control the market. It is only these seeds which can be legally sold under European law.
When this kind of legislation was adopted in every country in Europe, only a relatively few seeds could be legally sold. All the rest were effectively banned by the impact of the patents acquired by the multinationals.
The particular risk that we now face is that not only will the patents be made available effectively into private hands, the number of companies operating will decline. The companies get bigger and bigger, and are harder to control by national legislatures and parliaments. This results in increasing narrow control of this very vital area of human existence.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Victoria opened a new element in this debate with his closing remarks just now.
I wonder if he, who is learned in the law, could explain to me and to this House how it is that a government that claims that it is trying to open the world to freer trade, access to business, individual enterprise and so on, could possibly put forward a bill like this? It closed off access to plant genetic material and permits it to be monopolized by a few multinational corporations. How is the government's philosophy of free enterprise consistent with a bill that, in fact, restricts the ownership and control of most of the globe's genetic resources to a few multinational corporations, resident in the developed countries?

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Mackenzie. It almost invites me to launch into a discussion of how we got into free trade, into the GST and all the other issues which this government has foisted upon the Canadian people.
Let me, without extending this discussion too far off the subject, just simply say that this bill is entirely consistent with the philosophy of this government, that is to say, it will serve, in the final analysis, the interests of big business and of the large corporate power in this countiy and in other countries, particularly the United States.
When the crunch comes, that is the way this government operates on every single issue that comes before it. This is not a free enterprise government, this is a capitalist government. This is a government that responds to power in our society, power that is primarily resident in large corporations. When the big corporations came forward and said they wanted this bill, they got it. That is what has happened.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
The hon. member, speaking on plant breeders' rights, in my opinion has misrepresented the bill in the sense that this bill does not preclude the government or any organization from competing in plant breeding.
In fact, this bill will enhance and encourage this. If one wants to talk about the political philosophy of the NDP, we can look at some examples of 75 years of socialism in eastern Europe which has fallen flat and which is an example of the kind of thing that the NDP is recommending here in the House.
This does not preclude, in any way, the government from competing, whether it is at Swift Current, Saskatchewan, or whether it is at Indian Head or any of the areas
May 3, 1990

where plant breeding takes place and from where we have received some of our varieties.
Also, there is misrepresentation on the European situation. Some of these varieties were catalogued and, in fact, duplicated, as was raised earlier. We are really talking here about the NDP philosophy versus any private opportunity to enhance plant breeders' rights for the farmers and for better varieties of grain of which we have seen example after example.

Madam Speaker, before this bill goes through, the current situation is that anyone who wants to get into the business of breeding plants can do so. What they cannot do now is control, for commercial purposes, and sell the effect of their discovery in the same fashion that will be possible after this bill. On the surface it seems that after this bill passes everybody will think they can develop a new plant and become rich. The fact is, if I put the hon. member for Souris-Moose Mountain on the same rink with Wayne Gretzky, I do not think the comparison would be very easy.
You are putting everyone who is in the business of breeding plants in the same field with huge multinational corporations who will quickly buy up the developments that have taken place. My friend may think that that is a good system but I can assure him that the effect of that system will be that the economy, and particularly the economy in this area, will be increasingly controlled by the few at the expense of the people as a whole.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is over. Resuming debate with the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen- Merritt.

Madam Speaker, since I was elected to this place I have watched the plant breeders' rights legislation go through its various stages, first and second reading, report stage and now into third reading. I am from an agricultural area that deals in ground crops and fruits. I have received substantial correspondence from various constituents, and I can say that all of the correspondence was against the plant breeders' rights. They set out a number of reasons why. I would like to bring to the attention of the House some of what was said in some of those letters and petitions that were presented to me.
I became curious about the contents of this bill, exactly why my party opposes it, and why it was so upsetting to so many people within the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt. Why is there a a diversity of views from one area to the other?
Let us review the legislation in simple terms. First, the legislation governs only the varieties produced after the passage of the Plant Breeders' Rights Bill and the breeder of any new variety will hold exclusive rights to sell reproductive material of the variety for up to 18 years. On the surface, that appears to be desirable for an individual who establishes or breeds a new variety to get some benefit from that. If that was the purpose of this bill, perhaps it would be a laudable and agreeable piece of legislation.
However, if we look at what has happened in all of the other countries that have plant breeders' rights legisla-

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
tion, unfortunately that does not appear to be the case, as has been set out time and again by many of the debaters here today. It will increase the control of larger corporations in the area of plant breeding, seed stock et cetera. This, I would suggest, is not a desirable thing for Canada or for the world market, for that matter.
If someone wishes to sell a variety, they must have the breeder's permission and the breeder will have the right to receive royalties. As I said, this would not be so bad if it was the individual who was going to profit by it without being hurt.
Further, anyone can use a protected variety for plant breeding. To be granted a right, a variety must be new, distinct, uniform and stable. To protect the public interest, the breeder will not be able to restrict the supply of the variety to boost prices.
It has been suggested that a advisory committee with representatives from all sectors, including farmers, seed growers, plant breeders and seed merchants will be established to advise in the administration of the legislation.
It will be several years before all major Canadian crops are covered since each species will be researched before regulations are established for it. What are the objectives and expected benefits of this? We are told the legislation will stimulate investment in plant breeding in Canada. It is further argued that more improved varieties, both domestic and foreign, will be available for Canadian producers.
We are told the bill will permit the collection of royalties on Canadian varieties sold both in Canada and abroad, and the production in regions such as the maritimes will benefit from access to European cereal and potato varieties, that export sales will increase because of increased promotion of proprietary varieties, and that Canada will have a system compatible with other countries that have similar legislation, increasing the opportunity for export of Canadian varieties.
There are, admittedly, some major supporters of plant breeders' rights within Canada. In my mind, looking at the background and what has happened in other countries, the crux of the whole argument is who will control the seed stocks for our various plant varieties and how it will affect the majority of us as Canadians.
In researching this issue, it has been predicted that price of seed stocks will increase substantially. In one study in Manitoba, the prediction was that seed stocks would increase some three times. That causes some difficulty for farmers who already have their backs against the wall.
The major concern is the monopoly control that is apparent when we look at the history of plant breeders' rights throughout the world. There have been over 1,000 corporate takeovers of seed companies since 1969. There is a tie-in with the seed companies and the fertilizer and chemical companies. It appears that one ensures that there is control over the other. Many of the purchasers of these companies sell fertilizers and chemicals. In the 1970's, there were 30 companies that produced crop chemicals. Now there are about a dozen. Within a decade, the industry itself says that only six will remain.
It is interesting to note that under the European and United States plant breeders' rights legislation, 90 per cent of all seed patents are held by a handful of multinationals. That is the key, they are held by a handful of multinationals. It has been predicted that after the year 2000, 10 to 20 major corporations will dominate the seed market.
For myself and many of my constituents, this causes a major problem. The control of our basic food stocks by a few large multinational corporations sends shudders through me when I look at what is necessary for our very life on this planet. All of us need food to exist. If food is controlled, prices can be altered and increased or supplies can be held back for the increase in profits by multinationals. That is not something that I would like to see happen here in Canada, in particular, but I would not like to see it happen anywhere.
Let me turn now to some of the things that people in my riding have brought to my attention. I was presented with a petition which, unfortunately, is not in a form that is presentable to the House. Thirty-two people in the riding have sent it in to me to indicate their unhappiness with Bill C-15. They all feel that this gives the large conglomerates too much control of seeds. They are asking me personally to strongly oppose the bill. The petition simply states: "We, the undersigned, are against private ownership of genetic information and thusly we
May 3, 1990

oppose Bill C-15". It is signed by constituents throughout my riding in Penticton and in Naramata.
I also received a number of letters and I would like to share with the House one that was written to the Minister of Agriculture by Sharon Rempel of Keremeos in June, 1989. In part, she states:
This bill should be scrapped, and funding and research directed towards provincial plant breeding programs. Adequate gene bank facilities should be made available in all areas of the country, and continued free exchange of materials with other countries encouraged.
As a heritage seed saver I have heard from growers in countries with plant breeders' rights that access to old varieties becomes difficult, or even illegal. I do not want that in Canada. This aspect of a free market system is free only to the breeders, not to the rest of the population.
Please stop this bill before it is given final reading. I urge you to do so for the sake of sustainable agriculture, and the survival of genetic diversity in this country, and globally. Preservation of the plants should be done in the fields, not in the courts.
That letter was from Keremeos in the Similkameen Valley. I have a further letter from Naramata in the Okanagan in a similar vein from Daryl O'Neill who states:
I am writing to you to voice my strong opposition to C-15, the Plant Breeders' Rights Act. There is nothing more crucial to the welfare of a nation than its ability to feed itself, and I see that this bill, C-15, seriously compromises Canada's ability to do that, for the sake of multinational profits. Genetic diversity is threatened by the increasing reliance on over-developed, highly specialized hybrids, and the resultant loss of older standard varieties of plants. This could have disastrous consequences, as the 1970 corn blight in the U.S. indicates.
To conclude, I cannot express my extreme disappointment that your government would once again try to foist this odious piece of legislation upon us, for the benefit of corporate shareholders, to the detriment of Canadian citizens.
That letter was sent to the Minister of Agriculture on July 10, 1989.
Harry Nagel from Penticton writes:
Farming, especially smaller operations, is a marginal business. Keeping costs down is very important for growers. Is it not obvious that when the company that provides the seed also provides the agri-chemicals it is more likely to impact negatively on growers?
Although there are many other very good reasons for scrapping Bill C-15, my main concern is the promotion of chemical-dependent plant varieties and their apparent and hidden costs.
Government Orders
I encourage you to consider the impact on the smaller players by
this legislation.
That is a sample of some of the opposition in the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt. It puts this legislation in a broader perspective and outside of the area of plant breeders' rights. There must be a harmonization of the plant breeders and the plant breeders' rights with other countries, and particularly with the United States. I would like to digress for a moment and discuss the area in the Okanagan and Similkameen valleys that I come from and some of the difficulties we are already having.
As Mr. Nagel stated in his letter, farming is a marginal business, at best. Certainly, that appears to be the case throughout the Okanagan and Similkameen valleys, where more and more through the attempts at harmonization, through the free trade agreement and GATT, the farmers in my area have been hurt and this bill simply adds to that.
What we have now as a result of the free trade agreement and GATT are thousands of acres of empty lands where grapes used to be grown. Throughout the Okanagan and Similkameen valleys we now have acreage where soft fruits were previously grown which have been pulled out. Again, it is a matter of harmonization with the United States, doing what they see as necessary in order to make us more like our brothers, sisters and relatives across the border.
We are not like people in the United States. Certainly, we are related often by blood and otherwise, as I am myself. But we have a country of which we are proud. We have a country that has grown up through time and history with a proud heritage. The people of this country want to be able to viably produce the majority of our own food stocks, so that we can be somewhat independent of the rest of the world and assist other countries within the world.
What we see within my area is a breaking down of this ability. There is pressure on farmers to sell off their lands, whether it be for development, for housing, or for recreational areas, before they go broke. It is a moving away from the basic belief in the land. They cannot make a living. We are making it harder and harder for them by forcing them away from areas that they know well, whether it be soft fruit growing, farming, or the growing of cucumbers and tomatoes.

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
How do you take a 40 or 50 year old man or woman who has farmed one particular commodity all his or her life and tell them to strip the land and plant something else? You cannot do it, Madam Speaker. Since they were children, they have been growing that particular product and now they have to switch and look at the world market. It is very difficult for these people who have looked toward their retirement with very marginal profits throughout their lifetime and are looking forward to sitting back and relaxing a little bit in their retirement years. We have made it very difficult for them.
Farmers in the Okanagan, in the Fraser valley in British Columbia, Saanich in the lower island area of Vancouver Island, across the prairies, or Annapolis valley, it does not matter where, are running into the same problems time and time again. It is a problem of keeping up, making a living, and trying to overcome what nature throws at them. Now they have to struggle against a government that states that it is for farmers and is trying to help them. I would suggest that this is one more nail in the coffin of the farming community, one more put-down of the farmer. The potential of increasing the price of seeds for grain farmers, three times, ten times, or whatever in a marginal operation makes it very difficult for the farmer to make a living.
In conclusion, in the educational process of looking at this legislation, it is clear that although there are some who support this bill, it is not one that is of benefit to the individual farmer and therefore I speak against it today.

I listened attentively to my friend and I was impressed with his background, depth, knowledge and the insight he brings to this whole question of plant breeders' rights.
There is one area that rather puzzles me. I am a member of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and one of the areas that really interests me is this whole question of monopoly practices. In fact, statistics show that there have been 1,008 corporate take-overs of seed companies since 1969. Many of the purchasers also sell fertilizers and chemicals. In the 1970s, there were 30 companies that produced crop chemicals and today there is only a dozen. The industry itself states that within a decade there will probably only be about six remaining.
The minute we get this plant breeders' rights legislation passed, there are certain implications in terms of monopoly control of the seed companies and the seed business. In light of the fact that even this namby-pamby corporate take-over legislation that we have got has been ruled unconstitutional and now it is going to be appealed to the Supreme Court, I want to ask my colleague if he sees any significant problems for the people who depend on these various varieties of seeds to continue to get seed at a price that they can afford? Can he see a problem with the trend toward monopoly take-overs?

It is obvious that the member for Nickel Belt, being from a good agricultural area, has some of the education of the member from the Okanagan. The in depth knowledge that I have unfortunately simply scratches the surface of some of the speakers that we have had before us.
However, he turns to an area that is near and dear to our hearts and to the hearts of Canadians, which is the whole aspect of where this government is going and where it has gone in the past. For example, is this privatization for the sake of privatization. There is a whole public area here.
We have research stations and seed research funded publicly. We have scientists who now work for the federal government in various research areas, who are world renowned and are happy working within the system for the Canadian government, establishing new strains. That is one of the things I think there is a move toward, the ultimate privatization of that total area. I simply throw that out as a caution that there is that possibility.
What we have seen, and what I think the member for Nickel Belt has alluded to, is the monopolies that have been created. I sat as a substitute on his committee on the odd occasion and saw some of the mergers that have occurred over the last little while in many areas.
I also sat on the finance committee last fall and heard some of the confection manufacturers and others talk about being forced into mergers by legislation before the House of Commons, whether it is goods and service tax legislation or whether it is legislation on the free trade agreement. These large companies are becoming megacompanies.
May 3, 1990

More and more the control of our economy is falling into fewer and fewer hands. This is what the people of my riding are frightened by this particular legislation. What has alarmed me are the predictions that I heard throughout some of these hearings that I have been on, and now hearing it again in relation to this particular legislation. The control of our food stocks is falling into the hands of only a very few major corporations, and that has created problems. We have seen in the past that as we fall into the area of monopolies and do not have a competitive edge, prices have a tendency to go up. We have seen the prices of feed stocks go up for the farmers. I have stated that they will triple, but I understand that there are studies that show it to be substantially higher than that.
I believe'that when monopolies or control falls into very few hands, there will be major problems not only for farmers, but for the people of Canada in not only growing their food but obtaining their food at a reasonable price.

Madam Speaker, I appreciated and enjoyed the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt. I hope that his constituents are aware of the very active role he plays in this House in speaking on behalf of soft fruit and grape growers who have been hard hit by free trade.
Whenever there is a promotion of Canadian wines the member is on the front lines urging his colleagues to, in all moderation, enjoy the benefits of the production of his constituency. However, I would not want to over-ex-tend his knowledge of the agricultural field. I would, however, like to pursue some of the legal abilities which he does so obviously have.
One of the principal rationales that the government has presented as to why we have to adopt this legislation is that countries like the United States, Japan and others are pushing us internationally, particularly at the GATT negotiations, to adopt this legislation because of an argument that is being made in some parts of the world that things like genetic materials and life forms should be treated no differently in terms of international trade than things like the better mouse trap and intellectual property of different types such as movies.
I was wondering if the hon. member, as a lawyer or legislator, believes that there is some distinction that
Government Orders
needs to be made between the normal commerce that might go on in international trade and things that are so vital to our survival like genetic materials and the various life forms? Should a line be drawn? In fact, should we as the Canadian Parliament be drawing it by rejecting this whole trend?

It is clear that there is a major difference between some intellectual property rights, patents and copyrights that do not affect the very life blood of the people of Canada, or anywhere else in the world, for that matter. It is important to distinguish between the two. With this legislation we are working toward that very basis of life for people, our food stocks. When you start playing with food stocks, and you start playing with the patenting of our staff of life, then you are into a far different area in every way than you are with other intellectual property.

Madam Speaker, I join in debate of the Plant Breeders' Rights Act in opposition to its passage. I share the views of many in my province who are opposed to the introduction of plant breeders' rights in circumstances in which breeders of new crop varieties would enjoy exclusive rights in the commercial exportation of varieties of crops for a period of up to 18 years.
They oppose the notion that a holder of plant breeders' rights would be able to collect royalties on the sale of seed of the protected variety. They are also opposed to the concept of plant breeders' rights as they are so closely related to the patenting of industrial inventions, and legislation which covers plant breeders' rights in many other industrialized nations.
The notion that plants and seeds should be controlled and owned in the same way as industrial patents is not one which finds favour with many of those farmers in my riding. My riding comprises about 75 per cent of the dairy industry in Saskatchewan.
This legislation has been controversial and that is why its introduction has been delayed. It was a promise of the Conservative party in 1984, and it has taken until now before it has been introduced into this House. It is also well known that the Liberal party introduced legislation of a similar sort, but did not get very far with it either. We have seen that the Liberals, after committee hear-

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
ings on the bill, are now supporting this piece of government legislation.
The similarities between plant breeders' rights legislation and the drug patent legislation are quite clear to see. Once the Drug Patent Act was passed, the path was clear for the introduction of this legislation. Control of drugs which are necessary for the health of Canadians went into private hands. The government has now gone on to enable private interests to control the rights to make profits on plants, seeds and so on.
The drug patent legislation troubled many Canadians who use drugs and the consumer groups who represent them. It did so because of the fear of increased costs, and it did so because of the fear that if a drug manufacturer could control its interests in a particular drug that it invented, its long term control over that drug would preclude generic manufacturers in Canada from producing the same drug at a cheaper price. This would cut down on availability perhaps, but certainly on the opportunity for Canadians to pay less for those drugs.
Just as those who might potentially use drugs were concerned about the drug patent legislation and the potential price increase that that would give rise to, we have seen a reinforcement of the concerns raised by my party and other groups since the passage of the Drug Patent Act. For the same reason farmers, farm groups in Saskatchewan and those who are concerned about ownership of important natural resources in the world are concerned about the passage of plant breeders' rights legislation.
The issues are not only economic, although the government would prefer that we treat them in that way. They are also ethical, social and political, moral and ecological. The questions include: Who will do our research? Who wifi control the fruits of that research? Who will control our genetic resources, and are the resources of the world to be used by everyone or only by private corporations for their own benefit?
A question we sometimes do not ask enough is: What about those plant resources of the Third World which may be exploited by this practice? After all, most of the plant resources we use at the present time for our farming activities were originally found in the Third World. We took them without those Third World countries and farmers being paid for them. Now we are going to put the rights in the hands of private businesses to sell those seeds and plants back to those Third World countries from where we took them without payment in the first place.
There is concern from a broad range of individuals and groups, from genetic resources of our world, a coalition of church, farm labour, consumer groups, and non-government organizations. Membership includes the National Farmers' Union, OXFAM, the CLC, the Consumers' Association and the United Church of Canada. Many groups have been opposed to the passage of the plant breeders' rights legislation giving private interests control over something that was previously in the public domain.
In my province, as I mentioned, there are many who are opposed. Included is the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool which is opposed to the plant breeders' rights as they apply to major grains and oilseeds in western Canada. That organization, as you know, is the largest farm organization in the country. It represents farmers and attempts to ensure that they can obtain a living in spite of the federal government's agricultural policies. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool is opposed to the passage of this legislation as it applies to major grains and oilseeds for the reasons which I have generally indicated. I will now give more reasons in specific detail.
There are concerns about seed costs. At the moment, as we all know, fanners are very concerned about the input costs. They are at the present time trying to obtain financial assistance from the federal government to help plant their crop for the coming year. They are faced with high interest rates and they are faced with a low price for their product when completed. They are also concerned about reducing their cost of input as much as possible.
Seed costs at the moment represent about 4 per cent, for example, of Canadian wheat farmers' production costs. Europeans spend five times as much as this. There are suggestions, or predictions, by those in the seed industry that the farmers' share of costs will, in fact, rise to over 50 per cent in the next few years in Europe. A former minister of agriculture in Manitoba has suggested that with the passage of plant breeders' rights in Canada, seed costs in Manitoba could triple over the next decade as a result of this legislation.
May 3, 1990

Rather than attempting to address input costs for farmers, we have legislation from the government protecting private interests, ensuring that private interests control more of what was previously in the public domain, and in the process adding to the costs in quite a considerable level to farmers' input costs.
Allusion has been made to the problem of control of seeds. It has been indicated that some 1,000 corporate takeovers of seed companies have taken place since 1969. This indicates a considerable centralization and concentration of control by those who are in the business of selling seeds to our farmers.
Many of the purchasers of these seed companies also sell fertilizers and chemicals. Indeed, many of the developments that these companies are pursuing with regard to seeds are not to make them pest resistant as one would have hoped, but indeed pesticide or chemical resistant. We have those producers of fertilizers and chemicals buying companies which sell seeds and then ensuring that the development of those seeds is somehow compatible with their chemicals, rather than attempting to build into the seeds qualities which can resist the pests that we are concerned about. It is not a very ecological development in terms of how we develop our seed genetics.
In the 1970s there were 30 companies that produced farm chemicals, just as an example of increased concentration, and now there are about a dozen and perhaps within a decade the industry itself suggests that there might only be six. We will see a further concentration of those private organizations providing inputs to farmers.
As no doubt the government would be only too prepared to admit, increased concentration and lack of competition is likely to increase the price to farmers, making it ever more difficult for farmers to make a living and stay on the farm in Canada, making it more difficult for them to provide the food products that we so badly need.
If we wanted any more information or any more evidence of the concentration of control and the negative implications that that could have, we only need look to European and American jurisdictions where there is plant breeders' rights legislation. In those areas 90 per cent of all seed patents are held by a handful of multinational corporations. It has been forecast that by
Government Orders
the beginning of the next century, perhaps 10 to 20 major corporations in the world will dominate seed markets. It is only to the detriment of farmers and surely not to the benefit of farmers that lack of competition and the control over seed genetics cannot serve the Canadian farmers or the Canadian public.
In addition, seed and fertilizer companies are continuing to buy up and hold patents on seeds which make it hard for farmers in the Third World to get the seeds they want. It is harder to ensure that both in the Third World and in the prairies that farmers obtain the sorts of seeds that are suitable for the growing and soil conditions available to them. We are not seeing, in the concentration of ownership in seed corporations and we will not see it as a result of further concentration through the plant breeders' rights legislation, a development of seeds and products which will be suitable for Canadian farmers.
Many studies have been conducted, including a 1960 royal commission, which suggests it is not worth the economic benefits which might flow from plant breeders' rights legislation to have the legislation itself. Primarily, that is a result of criticisms of the industry because of the potential, as I have indicated, for massive concentration of the plant breeding industry by international corporations and primarily international chemical corporations.
We also have to be concerned about, as we are so often reminded, the diminution in our genetic base in the world. We often hear of the number of species which are lost to the world. It is important for us to maintain that genetic bank. In Canada we have a gene bank which protects many species which are important to us, in particular barley. There is considerable concern for the safety or the security of those genes. It is certainly the case that Canada's gene bank has been cited as one which does not provide the sort of security necessary to make sure that our genetic base in the world is maintained.
Even in a country such as ours, we are not able to protect the gene bank that we are responsible for. One other point which should be made strenuously and has been made before is that again we are bowing to pressure from Americans to do what their private corporations want. We are also bowing to pressure from the Japanese corporations and from other private interests around the world. It is one more push by the United States to have Canadians harmonize our standards and our approaches

May 3, 1990
Government Orders
with the standards of the United States. This is not to the benefit, of course, of Canadian farmers and Canadian consumers. It is time that we stood up to those pressures from American private corporations and governments acting on their behalf and take into account the interests of Canadian farmers and Canadian consumers. In coming to my final comments, I would like to point out the main drawbacks with this legislation and point out why the government should not be pursuing it in the way in which it is.
A great deal of research and activity in the plant breeding area is done in Canada by Agriculture Canada. There is a genuine fear that public sector plant breeding in Canada will decrease as governments reduce program funding in deference to increases in public sector investment and pushes more and more onto the private market.
There is also concern that the nature of public sector research will change with increased concentration on basic research and a decrease in actual variety development, in particular for crops such as wheat and canola. As a result of shifting the ownership of products onto private industry, as it is able to persuade Agriculture Canada to do, basic research rather than applied research will be done by private industry.
There is real concern that seed prices will rise considerably. There is concern that there will be restriction in the exchange of genetic stocks between breeders as competition increases. We have seen examples of that already where work is being done on particular plants and large corporations pressuring their friends in other large corporations to concentrate on some other development rather than the one of concern to the corporation in question.
We are concerned about the loss of the world's plant gene resources and that it will be accelerated as private industry promotes the cultivation of protected varieties in Third World countries. We are concerned as are many that a small number of multinational companies will dominate the Canadian seed industry as they have been doing through corporate take-overs, that they will integrate seed and farm chemical activities and develop and promote varieties whose performance is dependent upon the use of specific chemicals in which they specialize themselves and varieties whose performance is dependent upon various herbicides and fertilizers which are called into question and, as suggested by many, should be used less and less if we are really seriously concerned about the ecology of our planet.
Last, and perhaps more serious is the major criticism that Canada's food system will, as a result of plant breeders' rights legislation and following what we have seen in other countries, come more and more under the control of a small number of multinational corporations.
For example, in eastern Europe we have an example in which we see a society striving for more and more information and receiving more information, whereas in Canada we seem to have a government looking to concentrate ownership and information in such things as plants and seeds and in other areas as well.
This legislation, rather than opening up ownership and information, proposes to provide monopoly control which will limit access to information on genetic material. I think that is the wrong direction in which to go. We should be more concerned with making more available things such things as seeds and plants, which we have tended to do in the past, rather than making them more restrictive and in the ownership of a small number of corporations which then have to be purchased by farmers. We have seen increases in input costs. It will be to the detriment of farmers, Canadian consumers and indeed consumers of Canadian food products all over the world.
It seems to me it is the opposite direction in which we should be following. We should not be concentrating ownership and control of what had previously been public property. We should be making sure that access is more widely available. We might be able to manipulate genetic material, but we did not create it. Humans did not create it, and we should not receive compensation for something in which we have a minor role in assisting. There are interests for everyone all over the world in making sure that ownership of seeds and plants are more widely owned, and not more closely owned. Quite clearly, this legislation is a move in the wrong direction.

Mr. Speaker, in a publication called GROW, Genetic Resources for Our World, Volume II 1989,1 would like to bring to the member's attention a couple of
May 3, 1990

quotes, and ask him for comments and expansion with respect to the plant breeders' rights.
On the front page of that magazine, there is a quote: "If we believe in the right to a clean environment and that food is to share, then we cannot create a system which encourages ownership of life form, the most basic which is seed, by corporations whose primary motive is profit." I would like the member to comment on that.
There is a further quote on the last page of the article called "PBR, The Thin Edge of the Wedge, The Rationalization of Life Patenting". It indicates some excerpts from a book From Land to Mouth: Understanding the Food System by Brewster Kneen, Economist and Theologian. In one of these it states as follows: "It is then but a short step to the patenting, claiming the property rights of the modified human embryo, one that has been subject to gene therapy on the basis of need established as a result of amniocentesis on the embryo utero.
In other words, once the principle of intellectual property rights is accepted, there is no natural or inherent limit to the claims that can be made. Human characteristics could be patented and licensed for production just the way a McDonald's hamburger or a new lettuce plant could be".
Would the member like to comment on those two with respect to his impressions of where we are being led by the plant breeders' rights legislation?

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to respond to those two questions.
Let me take the last one first, the dangers of patents on life forms. Experts agree that it is very difficult to accurately define genetic substances in a way that effectively ensures that we do not move along a slippery slope towards patenting life forms, something which we would all be quite concerned about. I would agree with the member and the quote that he referred to. The plant breeders' rights legislation is something that we should be really quite concerned about, if we are concerned about the dangers of patenting life forms. I think we all are.
In terms of ownership of life forms being handed over to private corporations, we might refer to an example which has been in the public eye a great deal lately, and
Government Orders
represents a tragedy for Atlantic Canada. We can look at the developments which essentially placed the control of the fish stocks on the east coast in the hands of two large private corporations and observe what has happened to them. Those fish stocks were previously regarded as essentially public property which fishing people went to catch, and then to process.
By handing over the quotas to large corporations, those stocks became owned by those corporations. We have seen that stock, with the help of mismanagement by the federal governments over the last decade, fold to such an extent that we are now hearing from those in the fishing industry, including those whose lives depend almost totally on the fishing industry, that we should stop fishing. If we do not, we will end up by having no fish left there at all. Indeed, there are many examples of areas where there was previously a good deal of fish, and where now there are none.
We can look within our own country at what has happened when we have given private ownership over a life form to large corporations, and watched the way in which they have abused it. There is no doubt that we need to be very careful when we give large corporate interests-as we are going to do-control over plants and seeds. As experience in other countries which have with the plant breeders' rights legislation has shown, if we give ownership to large corporations they will use it only to ensure that they make profit and will not make sure that it is used to the best advantage of all Canadians and to all those who might otherwise have access to that resource.

speakeroldname: Hon. Frank Oberle (for the Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons) moved:
speechtext:
That the Standing Orders of the House of Commons be amended in the following manner:
1.	By adding the following new section to Standing Order 30:
"(7)(a) Notwithstanding Standing Order 24(3), if Private Members' Business is to be taken up on a day, other than a Monday, appointed for the consideration of the business of supply, the time provided therefor shall be delayed by one hour; provided that it shall be further delayed by the time required for the completion of any division arising out of the business of supply or any deferred division set down for that day. Upon the completion of Private Members' Business, the Speaker shall adjourn the House until the next sitting day.
(b)	Any recorded division demanded during the time provided for Private Members' Business pursuant to subsection (a) of this section shall be deferred in the manner set down in Standing Order 45(6) for proceedings on a Friday."
2.	By deleting sections (1) and (2) of Standing Order 87 and substituting the following therefor:
"87. (l)(a) At the beginning of a session, the Clerk of the House, acting on behalf of the Speaker, shall, within two sitting days of the placing on the Order Paper of separate items of Private Members' Business from at least twenty Members, notify the Members involved of the time, date and place of a random draw of twenty Members' names to establish the order of precedence for twenty separate items.
(b)	To the extent that there is a sufficient number of eligible motions and bills, the draw shall be conducted so that there shall be in the order of precedence an equal number of motions and public bills originating in the House of Commons.
(c)	The names of Members with bills and those of Members with motions shall be drawn separately to produce the appropriate number of bills and motions. The names first drawn separately shall then be drawn again together to determine the order of precedence for those items.
(d)	Not later than 6.00 o'clock p.m. (7.00 o'clock p.m. on a Monday and 3.00 o'clock p.m. on a Friday) on the second sitting day after the day on which the draw is conducted, each Member whose name has been drawn, and who has given notice of more than one motion, shall file with the Clerk an indication as to which motion is to be placed in the order of precedence. If a Member does not file such an indication within the time specified, the motion first placed by the Member on the Order Paper under Private Members' Business will be included in the order of precedence. This requirement applies equally to each Member whose name has been drawn for a public bill.
(2) The Clerk of the House, acting on behalf of the Speaker, shall, when necessary during a Session, conduct a random draw to establish an order of precedence for not more than ten additional items of Private Members' Business, in the manner set down in section (1). No Member having an item listed in the order of precedence at the time of the draw shall be eligible to have his or her name chosen. Not later than two sitting days prior to the conduct of the draw, the Clerk shall inform the Members involved of the time, date and place of the said draw."
3.	By deleting section (1) of Standing Order 92 and substituting the following therefor:
"92.(1) The Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections shall meet as soon as practicable after the order of precedence has been established pursuant to sections (1) and (2) of Standing Order 87, and from time to time thereafter, and may select after consultation with, among others, the Members proposing the items, not more than three motions and three bills from among the twenty items in the order of precedence and an appropriate number from among any subsequent items for which the order of precedence is established and such selected items shall be designated as "votable items". In making its selection, the Committee shall not take into account the number of Members jointly seconding an item, but shall allow the merits of the items alone to determine the selection and shall report thereon, from time to time. At no time shall there be


May 3, 1990

more than three motions and three bills among the selected items on the order of precedence."
4.	By deleting Standing Order 93 and substituting the following therefor:
"93. Unless previously disposed of, selected public bills at the second reading stage or selected motions shall receive not more than three hours of consideration and, unless previously disposed of, an item having been once considered, shall be dropped to the bottom of the order of precedence and again considered only when it reaches the top of the said order.
Provided that, unless otherwise disposed of, at not later than fifteen minutes before the end of the time provided for the consideration of the said item, any proceedings then before the House shall be interrupted and every question necessary to dispose of the selected motion or of the selected bill at the second reading stage, shall be put forthwith and successively without further debate or amendment."
5.	By deleting Standing Order 99 and substituting the following therefor.
"99. The proceedings on Private Members' Business shall not be suspended except as provided for in Standing Orders 30(4), 50(4), 52(14), 91 and 94(l)(b) or as otherwise specified by Special Order of this House. No Private Members' Business shall be taken up on days appointed for the consideration of business pursuant to Standing Orders 53 and 84(2) nor on days, other than Mondays, appointed for the consideration of business pursuant to Standing Order 81(16)."
That, notwithstanding Standing Order 93 as amended, any selected i1em which is now on the order of precedence and has received more that two hours and forty-five minutes of consideration receive not more that an additional forty-five minutes of consideration following which every question necessary to dispose of the said selected item shall be put forthwith and successively without further debate or amendment;
That the Clerk of the House, on behalf of the Speaker, conduct as soon as practicable a random draw of a sufficient number of names, notwithstanding Standing Order 87(2) as amended, to establish the order of precedence for ten motions and ten public bills originating in the House of Commons;
And that motion No. 3, dated March 6, 1990, appearing in the Order Paper under "Government Business" be deemed withdrawn.
And on the motion of Mr. Milliken, seconded by Mrs. Finestone,-That this question be now put.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not wish to take much time in this debate but I do wish to signal to the House of Commons that this Motion No. 6 is the result of the work of the Committee on Privileges, Elections and Procedure that have studied the issue of Private Members' Business. This is largely the recommendation that they had put forward.
Government Orders
I want to say that the significant part of this particular amendment is one that allows an opportunity to treat all back-benchers of this House equally. The basic thrust of this particular amendment, among other things, is that now in Private Members' Business, the member's name would be drawn rather than the item. Therefore, each member would have one opportunity to have his or her name drawn and it would then mean that all members of the House who are private members would be treated equally.
I also want to signal that we on this side of the House, the government, are very much in favour of this particular amendment and are quite happy to lend our support to it.

Madam Speaker, it is nearly 11 months ago now that I raised during Question Period the issue of the sale of Air Canada shares .to foreign investors.
I want to make a point to House leaders on both sides of the House that it has been an unconscionably long time since I asked my questions. However, I am delighted to have the opportunity to rise in the late show, although this event arises out of my question 11 months ago. I was put on a list, together with many other people, and of course my number came up today, something for which I am very grateful.
I say to the deputy government House Leader that I spent a little time in the Newfoundland House, and there we used to do it a little differently. There, anybody who was dissatisfied with a question had to give notice that day by four o'clock, and then was on the late show that day, if he or she was one of three. If there were more than three, the Speaker made a choice and the matter ended that particular day.
The advantage of that, of course, is that the subject being discussed has some relevance and currency, much more than it does right now, 11 months later. I say that because much of the issue that I raised that particular day, on June 12 last year, has since become ancient history.
The Air Canada deal is over and done with. The government has had its way. Anything I can say on that particular subject, the sale of shares to foreigners, is of course locking the barn door long after the horse has gone.
Adjournment Debate
Although this is not my purpose in rising, I would suggest in passing that the House leaders on both sides might want to look at finding a way to make the late show a little more current than they have had the tendency of being because of the circumstance that I have just described.
However, since I have the floor, and on a subject that is broadly related to the issue at hand, you will recall, Madam Speaker, that my particular interest in the matter of Air Canada flowed particularly from the awful and wrong decision by Air Canada to pull its jet service out of Stephenville as of last June.
Once that deed was done-and done in a not very commendable manner-I said to the president and to some of the senior officers of Air Canada on at least three occasions in their boardroom in Montreal, and in letters, that the way they did it is not a model way to conduct relations with people who have stood by them for 40 years, as is the case with the town of Stephenville in the Bay of St. George area of Newfoundland.
To add insult to injury, when the opportunity came for the airport of Stephenville to get a new jet service through a proposal by First Air of Ottawa, Air Canada also blocked that particular initiative, and focused on a particular issue in so doing. It focused on the question of whether or not so-called airline deregulation has not, in effect, created a duopoly situation in air transportation of this country where the two airlines, Canadian and of course Air Canada, can not only decide where they are not going to fly, but can also effectively decide that nobody else is going to fly there.
Through the mechanism of joint fare arrangements which all airlines have with each other, a company, in this case Air Canada, by refusing a joint fare arrangement with a particular carrier can effectively prevent that carrier from going into an airport. That is precisely what it did in the case of First Air and Stephenville.
Stephenville is a town that is far from beaten. Let me tell you, Madam Speaker, two things have flowed from that particular obnoxious act by Air Canada.
First, an initiative has been launched through the Competition Bureau which in time will bear fruit. The Competition Bureau right now is looking at the issue of whether Air Canada is in violation of the Competition Act by virtue of its action with respect to Stephenville, the action I have just described in effectively preventing another airline from going in and providing jet service.

May 3, 1990
Adjournment Debate
That is in the process, and I will let the House know more about it later.
The second thing that is happening is much happier. Thanks to the efforts of the town of Stephenville, the Chamber of Commerce, the whole leadership in the Bay of St. George area and southwestern Newfoundland generally-thanks to a massive effort-I am delighted to inform you, Madam Speaker, that as of last Sunday another airline, Air Atlantic, a connector airline of Canadian using the BAE-146, 70-passenger jet has begun jet service between Stephenville and Ottawa. On Monday of this week, 50 of my constituents from Stephenville who came on the inaugural flight were here in the gallery to witness the proceedings in this House and to say thank you to people, including people in government.
In particular I want to mention my good friend the now Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, who was then the Minister of State for Transport at the time when she took an initiative. I will submit that the initiative she was able to take was partly because of her knowledge, coming from an airport area, Hamilton South. We thanked her at a function the other night. I just want to say in passing that through her efforts and the efforts of many others, Stephenville is back on the map again in terms of jet service. These people came to thank her.
In conclusion, my purpose in giving notice 11 months ago has long since slipped away, like so many other things 11 months later. I make two points.
First, we ought to look at a rule change which would make this whole debate much more current.
Second, I rise because I want to send a signal to Air Canada that the fight is far from over. The fight will not be over until we get the assistance of this government to ensure that deregulation, whatever its good purpose is, should not be manipulated to serve the negative purpose of preventing small communities such as Stephenville from having a jet service through the duopoly that I have described.

Madam Speaker, during Question Period on March 14, I asked the Minister of State (Forestry) about forestry development agreements that had expired.
My questions were as follows, and I quote at page 9278 of Hansard:
Does the minister intend to renew these agreements? Where will he find the money, and how much does he intend to spend on these agreements?
Another question:
Where is the $1.1 billion promised by the Prime Minister and when will the new forestry agreements be renewed?
May 3, 1990

Madam Speaker, I was not satisfied with the answers given by the minister acting for the Minister of State (Forestry) on that particualar day.

As I mentioned, not being very satisfied with the answers I received, I decided to try to get more answers this evening.
Since coming to power in 1984, the government has claimed that it would create a forestry department, which it did. I must congratulate the government for that initiative. I think it was a step in the right direction.
The only problem with the forestry department, as I see it now, is that the government actually reduced the power of the forestry department across Canada. It reduced it by reducing the budget and by reducing personnel.
This is the week before National Forestry Week. When we talk about current topics this is a very current topic.
Last year, the year that the department received its full status, it suffered an 11.9 per cent budget cut and a personnel reduction of 3.5 per cent, roughly a reduction of $28 million.
If we look at this year's budget, we find another reduction of 31 per cent over last year's reduction, basically a reduction of $47.6 million.
Further, if we look in other departmental budgets we find further cuts. These are budgets, supposedly, from which funding for forestry agreements is supposed to come, the funding for co-operative agreements.
The new Department of Forestry Act does not provide the forestry minister with any clout. If we look at the act that was passed last year instituting this new department, we find that the forestry minister must go to other departments to get funding for those forestry agreements. Certainly he does not have much clout when it comes to forestry agreements.
When we discuss the forestry agreements, we can say that we have consensus here in the House. All my hon. colleagues in all three parties have reached a consensus on this one issue. The forestry Resource Development Agreements have been very beneficial right across Canada. There is no doubt about it. There are some negative things about them. Some things just do not work right.
Adjournment Debate
But, in general, the forestry agreements have been a success across Canada, and there is a need for more.
Last year, six of those agreements expired. Those in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta were terminated last year, supposedly at the end of the year. We asked the minister at that time to renew them as soon as possible. A couple were renewed. The ones with Nova Scotia and my home province of New Brunswick were renewed. In fact I am very proud to say that New Brunswick received a little more money than we expected. I am sure it will go to good use.
This year on March 31 we see three more major agreements have expired, especially the ones with the province of Quebec and the province of British Columbia. We know that the province of British Columbia has now committed funding to renew those agreements. So this is certainly a concern.
When we look a year later down the road, we see that seven of those agreements have not been renewed, which is cause for concern.
That brings me back to the questions that I asked on March 14, not too long ago, the questions I have asked in committee and the questions we asked last year when those earlier agreements had expired. We have asked the minister when he intends to renew the forestry agreements. We have asked him where he would find the money for their renewal and how much he intended to spend on them.
As well as asking those questions the other day, we also asked where was the $1.1 billion that the Prime Minister seems to have committed at a meeting not too long ago in Montreal with the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, as was reported in the media.
The response given by the minister was vague and did not provide a clear indication of the government's intentions with respect to the renewal of these agreements.
However, in all honesty, Madam Speaker, I must make sure that the people who are listening, as well as my hon. colleagues, that the Minister of Forestry was not in the House that day. With all justice to him, he was on government business. The answer I was hoping to get

May 3, 1990
Adjournment Debate
may not have been forthcoming because he was not available to give us all the details.
This is why I more or less was hoping that we would have more details this evening, which is why I have asked for this opportunity this evening.
Our country suffers from a backlog of unsatisfactory but restocked forest land, as was indicated in the estimates provided to the forestry subcommittee by the minister's own officials. That backlog consists of around 200,000 hectares every year. Those are the estimates this year.
It is imperative, it is very important-it is urgent-that the government get on with the job of renewing these agreements. It is these very agreements which have helped promote the forest sector right across the country. It is not enough, but without these forestry agreements in place it is certainly a negative step, especially this week being the week just before forestry week.
Given the forestry department's budget reductions and given the reductions in funding for all Economic Regional Development Agreements, what we want to know as members on the opposition side is this. Does the government intend to renew the forestry agreements which have expired? When will it do so? How much money does it intend to spend and from which budgets?
For instance not too long ago in the forestry subcommittee the minister mentioned to us that the B.C. funding would be available before seeding commenced. Well, seeding has commenced.
I also recognize the fact that if an agreement is signed it would probably be retroactive anyway. That is something that has happened in the past, and I recognize that.
I would ask that the government give us an indication tonight about those Forest Resource Development Agreements.

Madam Speaker, I rise in the House this evening because I was dissatisfied with the response I received from the minister responsible for the status of women on the issue of funding for REAL Women.
I asked her about the government's impending funding decision for that organization in light of a recent very offensive newsletter that had been issued by that group.
The Conservative government seems to have found ways to undermine the women's movement, and to undermine equality for women. One way it has done that was through having funded REAL Woman last year. Another way is that it has cut the funding for equalityseeking groups in our society. In fact, the decision to fund REAL Women last year came just before last year's budget decision to cut 15 per cent off the women's program.
I had to apply last year under the Access to Information Act about the government's decision to fund REAL Women. I could not get any information from the Secretary of State's office about that funding proposal.
This year another 15 per cent is gone from the women's program. This time the grassroots was attacked. Seventy-five women's centres across this country lost 100 per cent of their core funding.

The women's movement is simply asking for-demanding-economic and social justice for women. It is demanding true equality in our society for women.
When women, only a few decades ago, were fighting for the vote they were called all kinds of unsavoury names too. There was a movement of women against the suffragettes. There were women who did not want the vote and wanted to deprive other women of it too. There will always be a backlash against positive social change. The government is under no obligation to fund both the progressive and the regressive elements in our society.
In light of its own commitments to the international treaties it has signed, the government has an obligation to promote equality. That is what the women's program should do. That is why full funding for women's programs should be reinstated. Groups like REAL Women should never, never again be funded by any level of government.
I am very concerned about the disproportionate amount of influence that this organization appears to have, both within the federal level of government here and the provincial government of B.C. We know that they speak for very few people. People in Canada do not support those attitudes.
I ask again: Will the government guarantee that this anti-equality, anti-feminist, hate-mongering organization will never again receive government funding?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I want to congratulate the hon. member for Westminster-Burnaby who examined this question and produced, I would say, a pretty fair analysis.
I may recall, and I think she will understand from my reply that we are also very concerned, the operating criteria of the Women's Program of the Department of the Secretary of State.
To be eligible, women's volunteer organizations must have as their principal goal to promote the equality of women in Canadian society.
These organizations must respond to a need in the community, approach issues that are eligible for financial assistance under the Women's Program, demonstrate their ability to plan projects and bring them to fruition, have a good financial management system, involve their members in developing policy and use funds only for non-partisan activities.
In accordance with these criteria, the Department of the Secretary of State has set three priorities: economic equality, social justice and access and participation.
Last year, REAL Women obtained funding under those criteria. Until we have seen, after one year, whether the program for which funding was requested was in fact carried out as described, we will not know whether the criteria were net. Officers at the department are now analyzing the application, and based on the criteria and on what happened last year, Madam Speaker, they will decide whether the application for funding meets those criteria.
I can assure the hon. member for New Westminster- Burnaby (Ms. Black) that I will personally see to it that these criteria are enforced, and that the analyses made by departmental staff are reliable, so that we can find out whether or not this group deserves to be subsidized.
